sources.entry: pylint - A fully customizable source code analyzer.

summary.one_liner: Pylint is a static code analyser for Python that checks for errors, enforces coding standards, and flags code smells without running the code.
summary.what_it_does: Pylint analyses Python source without executing it, checking for errors, enforcing a coding standard, detecting code smells, and suggesting refactors. It infers the actual values of nodes using its internal representation (astroid), so it can catch cases like a module imported under a misleading alias. It is highly configurable, supports writing plugins for custom checks, and has an ecosystem of plugins for frameworks and third-party libraries. The README recommends starting with --errors-only during adoption and then progressively disabling or re-enabling convention and refactor messages. It also ships with two extra tools: pyreverse, which generates package and class diagrams, and symilar, a duplicate code finder.
use_cases: lint Python code for errors and style issues
enforce a coding standard in a project
find code smells and suggest refactors
add custom checks for internal libraries via plugins
generate UML-style package and class diagrams
how_to_run: pip install pylint[spelling]  (optional, enables spell checking via the enchant C library)
notable: Infers actual values of code nodes rather than trusting type hints, so it can detect misleading aliases such as a logging call under an argparse name
Highly configurable, with opinionated checks disabled by default that can be enabled
Supports custom plugins and has an ecosystem of framework plugins (e.g. pydantic, django)
Ships pyreverse diagram generator and symilar duplicate code finder
caveats: Slower than other linters because of its inference analysis
Third-party libraries are not always supported and may need a plugin
Can produce false positives; the README notes it is not smarter than the developer
